newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Ex-Amsterdam-N.America cargo rates firm in strong.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Amsterdam-N.America cargo rates firm in strong.

text.p: Business from Amsterdam to the Americas is proving very busy at the moment, according to a Reuters survey.
And generally, business is better than last year to North America, he said, largely due to strength of the dollar.
Dan de Wit, managing director of Speed, a company which bought most of Martinair's belly-hold capacity to North America, said exports to the U.S. are very strong at present.
Destinations the Schiphol-based wholesaler will sell from the Netherlands include San Francisco, Los Angeles and Toronto, he said.
"Exports from Europe to the U.S. are very strong. A lot of our clients will have dedicated allotments on the flights so they have guaranteed space," he said.
Much of the cargo to North America is perishable traffic including peppers, tomatoes and flowers, he said. The main season lasts from April until October.
In a separate deal, Wisbeen, a leading perishables and flower company, will sell Martinair's bellyhold capacity to New York.
The reason given for the booming market by all the Reuters sources is the strength of the U.S. dollar.
Cargo rates to the U.S. have also firmed-up. For instance Amsterdam-New York has increased to 1.80 guilders from 1.60 per kg and rates to Los Angeles have seen a ten cents increase.

Ton Jansen, the Netherlands cargo manager of Iberia Cargo said the increasingly busy Latin America market led Aerolineas Argentinas - in which Iberia has a stake - to double its freighter flights out of Maastricht Airport to Buenos Aires.
There are now two flights a week from the Dutch airport to the Argentinian capital and Iberia is reponsible for selling the service from the Netherlands.
"Rates are under pressure though," he said. There are also many telecommunications projects going on in Latin America, he said, with companies such as Ericsson and Philips exporting to the region.
Bolivia is picking up, as is Uruguay, he added. From June, Iberia will fly to Montevideo from Madrid.

Jansen said that rates are under pressure in Sao Paulo but higher rates can be gained from Montevideo. Iberia is trying to target smaller connsignments and destinations where better rates are available, he said.
Cargolux' Netherlands cargo manager, Peter Schoute said Latin America is holding up very well at the moment, with Buenos Aires, Santiago and Sau Paulo having full flights.
Regarding on the North American market, Scoute said that the west coast of the U.S. is also buoyant but the east coast destinations are a little bit slower, he added.
Fred Veenendaal of VIA, general sales agent for Air Canada said: "We are not complaining at the moment. But we do not have enough capacity so we are having to refuse cargo to Canada."
Again the strength of the dollar was the reason for the boom, he said.
Hi-tech goods, textiles and ships spares are amongst the exports to North America.
Traditionally, the flower and vegetable markets are providing a boost for the Dutch-American market at this time of the year.

For instance, Uzbekistan Airways will increase capacity ex- Netherlands from June 3. A twice-weekly A310 service to New York will be replaced with a Boeing 767-300 service, said Carlo de Haas, spokesman for Air Support, the general sales agent of Uzbekistan Airways in the Netherlands.
The service operates Tashkent-Amsterdam-New York.

A Burlington Air Express spokesman said April has been a busy month to the U.S., although these exports are not such a big part of its Dutch business as they used to be as the group continues to increase its global presence.
Jos van der Woensel, owner of Zygene, said that North America is now booming with waiting lists for space to North America, he said. Zygene represents Delta Airlines in the Netherlands.
Dutch-grown vegetables are keeping the Dutch-U.S. market very busy and this is likely to last till the year-end, with the U.S.'s currency strength driving demand,, he said.

Latin America too and especially Chile, is doing very well , added Van der Woensel. Zygene represents Lan Chile and he said the company had expected to see a slight dip in May but this has not happened.
"We are full to the roof going to Chile," he said.

Rates in the Latin American market to some destinations appear to be showing signs of pressure. Mexico, and Sao Paulo have dropped with Mexico showed the largest decline, when its ex-Netherlands rate fell to 3.30 guilders from 3.70 guilders. But Bogota has seen an increase.

Argentina, Brazil and Chile appear to be the strongest markets, he added. Often to Chile shippers have to book a week in advance, in order to get space, he said. Cargo to Chile includes: "Machinery, machinery and machinery, from medical to mining to telecommunications equipment," he added.
Brazil has not seen the enormous growth of the past few years, he said, although it is still a relatively strong market. There is also more interest in Uruguay, he said.

Van der Woensel ,who also represents Air Gabon, said traffic to Africa is more busy. He said the airline has attracted more traffic from Europe and it has expanded its services within Africa. Compared to many destinations in Africa, Libreville is also a reliable destination for cargo, he added, which could account for the airline's increasing business.

Burlington is also targeting several countries, one of which is South Africa. "South Africa is especially interesting at the moment with exports ranging from copying machines to electronic equipment," said the spokesman.

However, it appears that the South African rate is under pressure. Several airlines entered the market at the end of last year and the average rate is around 3.90 guilders to Johannesburg, although lower rates are available. --Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542-7706 Fax+5017
